Goings
gō'ĭngz
n. pl. (steps, journeyings, the course of a life — and in Micah, the eternal proceedings of the Son of God)
The verbal noun of go, Old English gan. In the KJV it renders Hebrew 'ashur and ma'gal, a step or track, and motsa'ah, a going forth or origin, and massa', a setting out on a journey.

Biblical Definition

Goings is the KJV's word for the whole course of a man's steps, and it is almost always used with a sense of who is holding him up. David prays, “Hold up my goings in thy paths, that my footsteps slip not” (Psa 17:5), and testifies to the answer in the great deliverance psalm: “He brought me up also out of an horrible pit, out of the miry clay, and set my feet upon a rock, and established my goings” (Psa 40:2). Solomon adds the corresponding warning — a man's way is not private: “the ways of man are before the eyes of the LORD, and he pondereth all his goings” (Pro 5:21), said in the middle of a chapter about the strange woman, where a man is most inclined to imagine himself unobserved. Numbers uses the word for the stages of the wilderness march, which Moses was commanded to write down (Num 33:2) — a record of forty years of going out and going in. And then Micah takes the word out of time altogether. Prophesying the birthplace of the Messiah in a village too small to be reckoned among the thousands of Judah, he says of the ruler who will come from it: “whose goings forth have been from of old, from everlasting” (Mic 5:2).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines goings as the act of moving, departure, or way of life and conduct; and in Scripture, the ways or doings of a person.

expand to see more

GOING, n. The act of walking or moving; departure; pregnancy.

GOINGS, n. plu. Ways; doings; behavior; the course of a person's life.

In Scripture, the goings of a man are his steps or his whole conduct, which the Lord observes and directs.

The goings out and comings in of Israel in the wilderness were written by Moses at the commandment of the Lord.

Goings forth, in Micah v. 2, denotes the eternal generation and procession of the Messiah.

Key Scripture

Psa 17:5 — "Hold up my goings in thy paths, that my footsteps slip not."

Psa 40:2 — "He brought me up also out of an horrible pit, out of the miry clay, and set my feet upon a rock, and established my goings."

Pro 5:21 — "For the ways of man are before the eyes of the LORD, and he pondereth all his goings."

Mic 5:2 — "But thou, Bethlehem Ephratah, though thou be little among the thousands of Judah, yet out of thee shall he come forth unto me that is to be ruler in Israel; whose goings forth have been from of old, from everlasting."

Modern Corruption

Mic 5:2 is reduced to a prediction of a birthplace; the second half of the verse asserts the eternal pre-existence of the child, and Arianism in every century has had to get around it.

expand to see more

Mic 5:2 is quoted every December for its first half and rarely for its second, which is the doctrinally decisive one. A ruler is to come out of Bethlehem — and the same ruler's “goings forth have been from of old, from everlasting.” The Hebrew miqqedem mime 'olam is as strong an expression of unbeginning existence as the language affords. The child who has a birthplace has no beginning. This is the doctrine the church confessed at Nicaea against Arius, that the Son is begotten, not made, of one substance with the Father, and it is the doctrine every unitarian movement since — Arian, Socinian, and modern — has had to explain away. Micah puts the two natures in one verse, seven centuries early: born in a village, and going forth from everlasting.

The second thing in the word is a doctrine of guidance, and it corrects a common anxiety. Christians ask how to find God's will as though their steps were their own to arrange and the difficulty were locating a hidden map. David's language is different: he asks God to hold up his goings, and reports that God established them, and Solomon says God pondereth them — weighs and levels them. The same book says it flatly: “A man's heart deviseth his way: but the LORD directeth his steps” (Pro 16:9). The believer's duty is obedience in the plain commanded things; the ordering of the course belongs to God, and He has never mislaid it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew 'ashur (H838), a step; ma'gal (H4570), a track or entrenchment; motsa'ah (H4163), a going forth, origin; massa' (H4550), a journey.

expand to see more

Hebrew 'ashur (H838) — a step, a going; the word of Psa 17:5 and Psa 40:2.

Hebrew ma'gal (H4570) — a track, a wagon-rut, a course of life; the word of Pro 5:21.

Hebrew motsa'ah (H4163) — a going forth, an origin; the plural of Mic 5:2.

Hebrew miqqedem (H6924) — from of old, from aforetime; the first of Micah's two eternity terms.

Hebrew 'olam (H5769) — the vanishing point, everlasting, eternity; the second.

Usage

"“Hold up my goings in thy paths” — a prayer for the steps themselves."

"“He pondereth all his goings” — a life weighed by God."

"“Whose goings forth have been from of old, from everlasting” — a child without a beginning."
